Borrowed from French ouverture. Doublet of аперту́ра (apertúra).

Borrowed from French phaéton, ultimately from the Ancient Greek Φαέθων (Phaéthōn).

parole.significato: delft, faience (type of tin-glazed earthenware ceramic)

parole.significato: bottle, vial, flask (usually of perfume, shampoo, cosmetics, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French flacon. Doublet of фиа́ско (fiásko) and фля́жка (fljážka).

parole.significato: lobby, foyer (in a theater, cinema, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French foyer. Omitting several steps, from Latin focus.

parole.significato: fort (fortified defensive structure stationed with troops)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fort. Further from Latin fortis.

parole.significato: franchise (authorization granted by a company to sell or distribute its goods or services in a certain area)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French frégate, itself from Italian fregata.

parole.significato: A medium or substance used for frying (e.g. fat or oil)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French friture (“frying, medium for frying, fritter”), ultimately from Late Latin *frīctūra (“frying”), from Latin frīgō (“to fry”).
Borrowed from French fronton, from Italian frontone.
From French phthore (an obsolete early synonym of fluor), from Ancient Greek φθορά (phthorá, “destruction, deterioration”), because of the corrosive action of hydrofluoric acid.

parole.significato: foie gras (fattened liver of geese or ducks)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French foie gras (literally “fat liver”).
Borrowed from French fougasse. Omitting several steps, from Latin focus.

Late 19th century after French verre de fougère, a certain quality grade of wine glasses, made from fougère (“fern”) ash, manufactured particularly in the town Fougères having its name from abundance in fern and later a glassware industry by reason of this fern presence.
Borrowed from French funiculaire. Further from Latin fūniculus + -ārius.
Borrowed from French fourrage, from Old French fourage, from Old French fuerre + -age. Further from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą + Latin -āticum. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-.

parole.significato: portable loading room, van, caravan, wagon, waggon, camion (a covered vehicle used for carrying goods)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fourgon. Further from Latin fūror, from Latin fūr. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (whence Russian брать (bratʹ)). Noncognate with Russian фу́ра (fúra) (which is паро́м (paróm) related instead).

parole.significato: an auxiliary material used in a production; fitting

parole.significato: reception with light refreshments eaten standing

parole.testo: Borrowed from French fuselage. Ultimately from Latin fūsus. Compare Russian веретенообра́зный (veretenoobráznyj).
From хла́дный (xládnyj) + -о- (-o-) + кровь (krovʹ) + -ие (-ije), a calque of French sang-froid.

Borrowed from French chorégraphie, from Ancient Greek χορεία (khoreía, “dance”) + -γραφίᾱ (-graphíā, “written form (of a word, etc.), spelling”).

parole.significato: chagrin, shagreen (type of leather or skin)
parole.testo: Calque of French La Peau de chagrin of Balzac.

parole.significato: shallot (a vegetable in the onion family)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French échalote or German Schalotte.
Ellipsis of шампа́нское вино́ (šampánskoje vinó), from French champagne, probably through German.

parole.significato: champignon, field mushroom, meadow mushroom (any mushroom of the genus Agaricus)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French shampooing, ultimately from Hindi चाँपो (cā̃po).

parole.significato: chance, prospect (chance for advancement, progress or profit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chance, from Latin *cadentia (cadēns (p.a.p. of cadō) + -ia).
Borrowed from French chansonnier, ultimately from Latin canō.

parole.significato: blackmail (payment of money exacted by means of intimidation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chantage, ultimately from Latin canō.

parole.significato: charabanc (a horse-drawn and then, later, motorized omnibus with open sides and, often, no roof)
charm (quality of inspiring delight or admiration)

Borrowed from French château, from Middle French chasteau, chastel, from Old French chastel, from Latin castellum.

parole.significato: masterpiece (piece of work that has been given much critical praise)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chef-d'œuvre. Displaced previous шедёвр (šedjóvr).

parole.significato: deck chair, beach chair (a folding chair)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French chef. Omitting several steps, from Latin caput (whence also капита́н (kapitán)).

parole.testo: Borrowed from French schibboleth /shibboleth, from Hebrew שִׁבֹּלֶת /שיבולת (shibólet).

parole.significato: chic, stylishness, ostentatious smartness, good style

parole.testo: Borrowed from French chenille. Doublet of шени́лл (šeníll).

parole.significato: blatantly obvious, poorly concealed (of a lie, secret, story plot, etc.)
parole.testo: Literally, “sewn with white thread”, referring to the use of white thread in sewing to temporarily tack cloth. Calque of French cousu de fil blanc.
Borrowed from French chiffre, from Medieval Latin cifra, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr). Doublet of цифра (cifra).

parole.significato: rude gesture in which the hand makes a fist and the thumb is stuck between the index and middle fingers, which indicate…
parole.testo: 17th century; perhaps from French chiche (“stingy, niggardly; also "I dare you!"”).
Borrowed from French chaussée, from Proto-Romance *calciāta.

parole.significato: driver (of an automobile, truck, bus, etc.; usually a paid professional)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chauffeur (literally “stoker, fireman”). Omitting several steps, from Latin calefaciō + -ātor/-tor.

parole.significato: flirt, a thing going on, hanky-panky, slap and tickle

From French évacuation, from Latin evacuatio.
Borrowed from French existentialisme, from Latin existentia.

Borrowed from French écran. Doublet of ши́рма (šírma).

parole.significato: something that is considered exceptional, exclusive, one of a kind

parole.testo: Borrowed from French exploitation. Compare Ukrainian експлуата́ція (ekspluatácija).

parole.significato: eccentric (person who does not behave like others)
parole.testo: Via French excentrique, from Medieval Latin excentricus, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros, “not having the earth as the center of an orbit”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “point”).

Borrowed from French épique (matching the feminine gender) and/or combined with Latin epicus (matching the stress).
Borrowed from French escadre, itself from Italian squadra.

parole.significato: late 19th or early 20th century pre-dreadnought battleship designed to operate as part of a squadron

parole.testo: Borrowed from French escadron, itself from Italian squadrone.

parole.significato: escort (accompanying group of soldiers, guards, etc.)

parole.significato: bookshelf, bookcase, whatnot, etagere (a piece of furniture with open shelves for displaying ornaments or books)

scaffold (elevated platform on which a criminal is executed)

From я́сный (jásnyj, “clear”) + -о- (-o-) + ви́дящий (vídjaščij, “seeing”), calque of French clairvoyant.
Abbreviation of French numéro, from Latin numerō (ablative of numerus).
